title: Batch-slice admission + partial KV materialization for OOM resilience
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Sudden OOMs during bursty traffic cause request drops and model fallbacks that significantly degrade output quality. Root cause analysis shows bursts with long prefixes fill KV cache and transiently push GPU memory past safe thresholds. Existing strategies either evict aggressively (hurting latency/quality) or fall back to smaller models too late.
goal: Implement a request admission + partial KV materialization strategy that prevents transient OOMs by shaping batches at admission time and allowing low-cost 'partial materialization' of KV for low-priority or long-prefix requests. The feature should reduce OOM incidents by >= 80% for tail bursts while keeping end-to-end 95th latency increase under 12% and quality regression <= 3% (measured on our smoke prompts set).
acceptance_criteria: 1) Admission controller enforces batch-slice budgets that keep per-GPU reserved headroom; 2) Partial KV path materializes only recent n prefix layers for low-priority requests and fetches rest lazily without blocking fast-path tokens; 3) Chaos test (burst replay) shows >=80% reduction in OOM frequency compared to baseline; 4) Regression tests for top-10 customer prompts show <3% quality drift; 5) Metrics emitted to console dashboards (oom_count, partial_kv_hits, admission_throttles) and alerts configured.
design_summary: We introduce a Batch-Slice Admission Controller that computes an admission budget per batch window based on active KV occupancy estimates and a lightweight GPU headroom model. Requests are tagged with a materialization class (full | partial | metadata-only) at admission. Partial materialization stores only last-K attention states and shortens KV tensors for long prefixes, with a transparent lazy-fill that backfills full KV asynchronously when GPU headroom is available. Admission decisions prefer partial materialization for long-prefix or low-priority requests and will queue/hedge requests to avoid immediate model fallback unless latency SLOs are violated.
tradeoffs: Partial materialization reduces memory pressure at the cost of additional complexity and potential small quality degradation for partial requests. There is added scheduling jitter from lazy backfills and hedged requeues. We choose simpler conservative heuristics for initial rollout to limit surface area; future work may add learned admission policies.
implementation_plan: 1) Add headroom estimator and admission controller hook in serving runtime (Marco, 2d prototype). 2) Add 'materialization class' metadata to Request proto and wire through kernel paths (Marco + Priya, 4d). 3) Implement partial KV serialization format and lazy-fill microtask (Priya, 5d). 4) Add metrics and tracing spans; dashboard and alert (SRE lead: Dan, 3d). 5) Internal canary with 5% traffic -> 25% -> 100% with rollback triggers. 6) Post-mortem and perf tuning.
testing_plan: Unit tests for materialization boundaries; integration tests with controlled KV occupancy; chaos test that replays burst traces from prod 2025-02-11 incident; A/B with control group for quality regression on smoke prompts; automated end-to-end to validate no deadlocks in lazy backfill.
rollout_plan: Stage 1: rollout to canary fleet (5%) with 'admission=off' default; Stage 2: enable admission controller in partial mode for low-priority traffic only (25%); Stage 3: widen to 100% with throttles tuned. Rollback: feature flag to disable partial-path and admission decisions. Escalation: if OOMs remain above threshold, revert admission changes and switch to conservative evict-only mode.
monitoring_and_alerts: Emit metrics: runtime.admission.throttles, runtime.partial_kv.materialized_bytes, runtime.partial_kv.backfill_latency_ms, runtime.oom.count. Dashboards: canary vs baseline comparison, headroom over time, partial_kv hit-rate. Alerts: oom.count > 1/week per node in canary; backfill_latency_ms P95 > 500ms.
open_questions: What's the right default K for partial materialization across different model families?
Should partial materialization be allowed for high-tier enterprise customers or disabled by default?
How to account for pinned KV entries (hot tokens) in headroom estimator?
risks: Increased scheduling complexity could introduce latency jitter
Edge-case deadlocks if lazy backfill tasks overwhelm IO path
mitigations: Start with conservative K=2 and widen after A/B testing
Expose customer-level toggle to disable partial path
Limit concurrent lazy backfills per GPU and add backpressure to admission controller
